IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01692

“The human kernel is the heart (qalb, the ‘Abraham of one's being’); and the kernel of the kernel is the latîfat al-anâ’îya”—the subtle center of the true Self, the pearl contained in the latîfat al-haqqîya, the pure mirror of the divine Face—“which I shall explain to you later.” Elsewhere the shaykh speaks of the circles formed by waves on the sea.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01693

But rather than fall back on the easy comparison—so commonplace as to be irritating—favored by pseudo-philosophical monisms that hastily confuse different levels of being (“the waves arise and disappear; the sea remains”), Semnânî wants us to understand something else. There are visible forms: the circles (dawâ’ir) made by the movement of the sea's surface. They appear for an instant and vanish. These correspond to earthly, physical, perishable bodies.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01694

But there are also the haqâ’iq: the true Realities, the metaphysical realities of those forms—their essences, the substantial and formative Ideas of those fleeting circles, which are conscious of their own perfection or deficiency. These correspond to the acquired spiritual bodies, which do not perish.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01695

Many hadith refer to this subtle body. One says: “The spirits of the martyrs”—or “truthful witnesses”—“are in the crop of a Green Bird. They have lamps (qanâdil) hanging from the Throne. They roam through Paradise as they please and then return to those lamps.” The lamps, the shaykh explains, allude to the “acquired spiritual body,” purified and extracted from the Stone of the perishable physical body—an unmistakably alchemical image.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01696

Just as, in this life, the visionary's spirit (sâhib al-wâqi’a) freely wanders through the garden of the Mystery and then returns to its physical body, so the spirits of the martyrs and the Elect wander at will through the dwelling places of the Malakût and the Jabarût, through the divine Presences (hazârât) of the Lâhût, and then return to their “Throne-bodies” (abdân ’arshîya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01697

For his part, the fourth Imam of Shiism, Zayn al-’Âbidîn, when asked about the death of the physical body and the assumption of the subtle body, offered this beautiful comparison: “For the true believer, it is like taking off a filthy, lice-ridden garment and breaking heavy fetters and chains, only to exchange them for the most splendid robe, steeped in perfume, the lightest of vehicles, and a dwelling more delightful than any other. For the unbeliever, it is like taking off a splendid, fragrant garment and leaving a delightful home, only to receive in exchange the foulest and coarsest clothes, and the most desolate dwelling.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01698

But we must go further. What is at issue is not simply the lesser resurrection (qiyâmat soghrâ) understood as exitus, the event of physical death. The “lesser resurrection” is first and foremost initiatory death. This conviction is central, for example, to the reformed Ismailism of Alamût as a religion of resurrection.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01699

But it is found wherever initiatory death has been seriously contemplated, for it implies that the later event of physical death becomes a mere episode of little consequence: the outcome has already been decided. The idea follows from the Prophet's own invitation, repeated endlessly by the Sufis in a hadith: “Die before you die.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01700

The invitation means that “voluntary death” (mawt ikhtiyârî)—which is spiritual resurrection—must come before natural death if natural death is truly to be an exitus: a departure and passage into another world. For Semnânî, the command means: “Die willingly to worldly and bodily pleasures, so that with your inward eye you may behold, in the world of the Mystery, what you believe in.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01701

“For whoever has died this death has already seen his resurrection arise.” This, then, is initiatory death, the passage through which every spiritual initiation leads. And because such death is itself already resurrection, it gives the mystic here and now the privilege enjoyed by the spirits sheltered “in the crop of the Green Bird.” Like them, the mystic's spirit travels freely through the worlds of the Jabarût and the Malakût, then returns to the natural physical body, just as in the next world it will return to its “Throne-body.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01702

The image of the bird sheltering the delicate, subtle being of the spirits is no accident. It inspires another beautiful symbol through which Semnânî explains the formation of the imperishable subtle body (latîfa bâqiya). Recall how Suhrawardî interpreted the episode of Zâl, fed and raised by the Simorgh, the legendary bird elsewhere identified with the dove, emblem of the Holy Spirit (Book II, chapter V, above). By transferring the symbol of the cosmic egg to the human microcosm, Semnânî offers this comparison.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01703

The microcosmic egg, made up of the substance of Form and the substance of Matter, is the physical organism, the body “set in place” at the birth of the individual (jism maj’ûl). “Then God commands the Spirit, or the Soul—choose whichever name you prefer—to give off its warmth and brood over the egg until the chick's form (haykal) is fully developed. Then he commands it to break the egg, and it breaks the shell with its beak.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01704

“The chick emerges from its shell: that is, from the physical body, whose nature corresponds to that of the earthly world, and to the state obscured by the ambiguity of past and future. Neither past nor future has any true existence apart from the passing present (hâl, the nunc of zamân âfâqî, the continuous physical time measured by the movements of the stars; see Book I, chapter IV, § 5).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01705

“To preoccupy oneself with these things is mere amusement and play. The chick then enters the orchard of the other world, signifying a state free from the ambiguity of past and future”—the time proper to the soul, zamân anfosî. “It takes flight into the depths of space, enjoying gentle delight if its acquired body is complete, a body of light; otherwise it suffers all the torments of Gehenna.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01706

Semnânî has only to clarify symbols that are already transparent. The chick's fully formed body is precisely the acquired body: the spiritual body hatched from the earthly body through the brooding warmth of the bird that is the Holy Spirit. The beak that breaks the shell and sets the chick free is the Angel of Death—first of all, initiatory death, since the mere occurrence of physical death is by no means enough in itself to signal this resurrection. “I have used this comparison,” our shaykh concludes, “for someone who does not yet know the mystery. Anyone looking for signs will find in it a way to infer the invisible from the visible.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01707

“But the secret of this comparison cannot be understood until one has understood…”—in other words, until one has grasped Semnânî's entire cosmological scheme. How is this subtle body formed—the imperishable envelope of the divine Self, the theophanic Self that mirrors divinity, the child of the “Abraham of your being”? To understand, we must follow in detail Semnânî's account of the world, in which, drawing on earlier theosophical teachings, he traces the psycho-cosmic formation of the organs of subtle physiology, or latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01708

From the center of being in its oneness and from the centers in which beings unfold in their multiplicity, energies issue beyond—and even prior to—the cosmos described by celestial physics. These energies reach the organs of subtle physiology directly. And within the mystic, these organs of the immortal body are more, and greater, than the “stars of his destiny” (Schiller): they are the “prophets of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01709
Thus, in the secret depths of the origins of things, we can see where esoteric interpretation and mystical anthropology are joined.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01710

We can understand how the “inward unfolding of meaning,” advancing together with the progressive growth of the immortal body, reaches its fulfillment when that body has attained its full prophetic stature.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01711

It is this fullness of stature that spiritual seekers in East and West have pursued, confronting—in Islam as in Christianity, despite their small numbers—the same powers of this world. Perhaps the day we recognize the hidden kinship between these spiritual families, the study of religion will undergo a change like the one now breaking down the barriers between the physical and psychological sciences, between the sciences of matter and those of spirit. It will require a complete renewal of what we have been accustomed to call “humanism.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01712

Yet whatever unpredictable shape that new humanism takes, a Semnânî will certainly have something to say to it, insofar as he has persuaded the Sufi that the only thing to fear in this world is not being cast, by some dialectic he does not understand, into what some of our contemporaries call the “dustbin of history”—the only Hell imaginable within a desacralized mythology of the “meaning of history.” No. What a Sufi has to fear is falling behind his own true being, coming to a standstill that makes him miss its inner meaning, and so becoming a stillborn soul in the world beyond.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s6
6. The Psycho-Cosmic Formation of the Organs of Subtle Physiology
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01713

To escape this failure to keep pace with oneself is, for the spiritual seeker, to attain the full stature of one's being. We said a few lines ago that the secret of the growth of this immortal stature cannot be understood without reference to the psycho-cosmic process by which the organs of subtle physiology—the “prophets of your being”—come into existence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01714

Here too, we must grasp at least the broad outlines of Semnânî's metaphysics of being and his account of the world's origin. “Psycho-cosmic formation” means that each organ of the “subtle body,” each organ of the spiritual entity, originates in a fusion of cosmic energies, apportioned differently to each organ, which becomes a kind of condensation of those energies. We therefore need to know where these energies come from; and to do that, we must trace their metaphysical origins.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01715

Here too Semnânî knew he was doing something original. “It is this,” he writes, “that God was pleased to inspire in my heart, thirsting for the true Realities (haqâ’iq). Before me, it had occurred to no one—not to the ancient philosophers, nor to our spiritual masters (Awliyâ al-Dîn)… I say this while fully recognizing the eminence of our spiritual masters. It should cause no surprise if God sometimes reveals to a disciple a subtle reality that escaped his master… This does not mean that the disciple is independent of his master.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01716

“Far from it: it was the master who gave him the capacity to receive this inspiration, through the very gift that made him a spiritual guide.” Semnânî's metaphysics of being belongs to a line of thought in which we later encounter Rajab Borsî, Rajab ’Alî Tabrîzî, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, and others. In brief, this metaphysics cannot simply identify being that is truly “Being” (al-wojûd al-haqq) with absolute being (wojûd motlaq).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01717

For if that being is absolute—released from every condition—this presupposes a motliq, the one who releases it from those conditions; and it is this motliq that is Being in the truest sense, so fully so that it transcends even our category of being. Philosophers have generally begun by taking being as already given, along with the principle of being from which they derive Intelligence (Nous) as the first Emanation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01718

Just as Proclus's interpretation of Plato seeks, beyond Nous, the One that transcends being, Semnânî seeks the first metaphysical realities, which he calls the Awwaliyât. Beyond the first One (al-wâhid), beyond Nous as the arithmetically first unit in the series of numbers, there is the absolute One, which in its unique oneness is, metaphysically, the Solitary One (al-Ahad). “Understanding,” he writes, “the first realities that precede the existence of Intelligence (Nous) is a much more obscure matter.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01719

“Because of its hiddenness, the philosophers (falâsifa) have neglected it, despite the subtlety of their speculation, the abundance of their meditation, their long lives, their withdrawal from outward company, their exclusive concern with attaining the true Realities (haqâ’iq) of things, their diligent spiritual training, and the turning of their inward being toward their Lord so as to meet him. These secrets can be known only through light borrowed from the Niche of the prophethood of the Seal of the Prophets.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01720
I. The Awwaliyât, or First Realities
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01721

This “Niche of Prophethood” is the source from which Semnânî intends to derive all genuine knowledge of the first realities (awwaliyât). He is particularly conscious of his originality in using the celebrated hadith of the “Hidden Treasure” as the foundation for deriving the first metaphysical principles, and in analyzing the three “descents” that lie at the very origin of being and of being's manifestation. The divine Essence in itself (dhât) certainly transcends every interpretation, allusion, or metaphor.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01722

Yet as soon as we speak of it otherwise than by negation—the via negativa—we are compelled at least to conceive of it as having being. This is already the first “descent”: for us to speak of the Principle, which is beyond being (hyperousion), it must “descend” to the level of being. And it is through this very “descent” that we can understand how what is beyond being brings being into existence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01723

Indeed, at this level that is all we can say: by being, it makes other things be; it is al-mûjid, the giver of existence. At the second “descent,” we can conceive how this Essence, in being what it is, brings into being attributes essential to it—immanent, not directed outward, and revealing it to itself (tajallî sifât dhâtîya). And because it is known to itself, it yearns to be known by others. These attributes constitute its innermost life in solitary oneness; they are called the Attributes of Life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01724

Then, in a third “descent,” the Essence does what belongs to its very being: it commands beings into existence and brings forth the Emanation of its existence-giving act (fayz ijâdî). This is no longer a divine self-revelation to itself, but a revelation to others: Light, the fullness of its life, the disclosure of its being. This third descent marks the passage from the “Attributes of Life” to the “Attributes of Light,” from “attributes of essence” to “operative attributes” (sifât fi’lîya). Semnânî asks us to contemplate these three aspects in the three phases described by the famous hadith of the “Hidden Treasure.” His meditation amounts, in a sense, to a phenomenology of the first principles in Semnânî's own terms.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01725

“(a) In the words I was a Hidden Treasure, seek the secret of the point of pure Essentiality (noqtat al-dhâtîya). (b) In the words I loved to be known, seek the secret of the point of solitary Oneness (noqtat al-ahadîya). (c) In the words Then I created the world, seek the point of Unity capable of unfolding into multiplicity (noqtat al-wâhidîya).” Semnânî is justified in appealing to Sufi metaphysics, already found in Sahl Tostarî (d. 283/896), which carefully distinguishes qualitative, metaphysical oneness (al-ahad) from quantitative, numerical unity (al-wâhid). He then returns to the three phases to develop his analysis in detail.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01726

(a) The first phase is already a first “descent” (nazlat) from the “depth of the Cloud” (bâtin al-’amâ’). Already al-Haqq, the Divine Reality, has “descended” so as to be—to be the “Hidden Treasure.” To be this Hidden Treasure is its act of being for itself, uniquely and absolutely its own. So absolute is this uniqueness that, unlike all the Attributes, each of which has its own Name by which it is designated, or even given a distinct personal reality, “being” (wojûd) has no name other than itself: possessing itself, being for itself what it is, with reference to nothing beyond itself—dhât, the Essence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01727

(b) The second phase—I loved to be known—marks the second “descent,” to the essential Attributes immanent in the divine act of being, in its manifestation (tajallî) to itself and for itself. Here the Divine is at once the first Knower and the first Known; and the joy it takes in being known will become the motive for the divine manifestation of Creation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01728

Four “dimensions” of intelligibility now come into view. (1) The divine Being knows its own being: this is the attribute of Life, and hence the divine Name, the Living. (2) The divine Being knows the perfection and glory of its own being: this is the attribute of Hearing, and hence the divine Name, the Hearing. (3) The divine Being knows its own beauty: this is the attribute of Vision, and hence the divine Name, the Seeing. (4) The Divine knows that its being deserves to be glorified: this is the attribute of the Word (Kalâm), and hence the divine Name, the Speaking.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01729

These four attributes belong to the divine Being in its oneness, in what it is in itself and for itself, simply by virtue of being, without reference to any other being brought forth by its Command. They are the attributes of its Essence in the act of being (sifât dhâtîya wojûdîya): immanent attributes, not directed outward, attributes of divine Life in its intimacy. Certainly these Attributes of Life will have their projections, their “shadows” (zill), their forms of manifestation (mazhar), among the Attributes of Light at the “third descent.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01730

But at this stage (1) hearing involves only perceiving what proceeds from the subject who “speaks,” or inwardly expresses what lies within its own being; it presupposes no listeners. (2) Vision is the pure perception of what is inward (bâtin), without implying an outward object (zâhir). (3) The Word is speech uttered inwardly and inscribed on the “mental Tablet” (Lawh ma’nawî); it need not be spoken outwardly, ad extra, or inscribed on an “objective Tablet” (Lawh sûrî). (4) Life means the perpetuity and continuity of the Living One's knowledge of itself, the eternity of its Self in its oneness, understood as a quality that does not pass outward into an action upon something else.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01731

(c) The third phase—Then I created creatures so as to be known—marks the third “descent.” Here the “Hidden Treasure,” moved by love of being known, creates—commands into existence, KN, Esto, “Be!”—beings that will know it. In them its “operative” attributes manifest its essential Attributes of Life. Bringing beings into existence turns what were initially inward, self-contained qualities into actions directed outward—the active or “energetic” voice of the Greek verb—and transforms divine states into divine operations, or theophanies. All this is designated by the name and attribute of Light.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01732

Light's outpouring is this “third descent”: the bursting forth of divine manifestations from the center of Unity, no longer the oneness of the Solitary One, but Unity capable of unfolding into multiplicity—the first among the countable unities that follow it. Since nothing can be received from the center of pure Essence (noqtat dhâtîya) except through the intermediary of the First Unity of countable beings (noqtat wâhidîya), this center of Light, Life, and Being is what we have seen to be the condition of the higher latîfa. The hypostasis of Intelligence will exercise this “vicegerent” function (khilâfat), mediating between the center of oneness—the pure Essence—and multiplicity.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01733

Now, just as the divine Being's manifestation to itself and for itself has four intelligible dimensions, so too does the manifestation of God in and through Creation. This is an outpouring of light in which the divine Being is revealed to itself through the knowledge that beings have of it. This theophany also presents four dimensions of intelligibility (i’tibâr), each corresponding to and manifesting one of the previous four: (1) Light knows itself: the attribute of Knowledge. (2) It knows what is other than itself: the attribute of Will. (3) It is known by itself: the attribute of Power. (4) It is known by what is other than itself: the attribute of Wisdom.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01734

These Attributes of Light, understood as attributes of divine action and manifestation, are no longer merely states inherent in an essence, as in the preceding group of four. They involve a relation and therefore require a second term—and in the very act of requiring it, they bring it into being, since it is what they accomplish or effect (the maf’ûl of their fi’l, the factum of their facere). As acts or operations, they are Emanations, Outpourings (foyûz).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01735

But we must not imagine a material substance spilling outward and being divided into ever smaller portions. Rather, Semnânî tells us—significantly adopting Suhrawardî's vocabulary—we should imagine the radiance of a rising Light (ishrâq nûrî).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01736

At this point in the analysis, the four awwaliyât, or first realities, come into view. Just as Semnânî used the hadith of the “Hidden Treasure” to distinguish the three “descents” of being, so he turns to another equally famous hadith—or, more precisely, to four forms of the same hadith—to identify the moment when the One gives way to the Many. These four forms are often cited merely as alternative versions. Here, however, each fulfills an essential function. The four ways in which the Prophet expresses the secret of the first Creation are as follows.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01737

1) “The first thing God created was the Pen (Qalam).” According to our shaykh, this is the level of the active function (martabat al-fâ’ilîya). Since the divine manifestation is pictured as “cosmic writing,” this is the place of origin, the “rising point” (matla’) of the Book. The Pen is the projection or emanation of the attribute of Knowledge (the third descent, phase c, above).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01738

2) “The first thing God created was my Spirit”—that is, the Rûh Ahmadi, the Ahmadian Spirit (the glorified one, periklytos). This is the level of the primordial Inkwell (dawât, martabat dawâtîya), containing the primal matter of all Creation, spiritual and bodily alike, subtle and dense, transparent and opaque. The Rûh Ahmadi, or Inkwell, is the projection or emanation of the attribute of Will.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01739

3) “The first thing God created was my Light”—that is, the Nûr mohammadî, the Muhammadan Light. This too is the primal matter of all Creation, the luminous Ink contained in the Inkwell that is the Spirit. Both the Spirit of this Light and the Light of this Spirit are described as Ahmadî or Mohammadî: the archetype of primordial Glory (doxa), of which the person of the Prophet was the earthly appearance or manifestation. The Muhammadan Light, the luminous Ink, emanates from the attribute of Power.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01740

4) “The first thing God created was Intelligence” (’Aql, Nous). Intelligence is what bears the writing made by the luminous Ink, and is therefore called the Tablet (Lawh). It is the projection or emanation of the attribute of Wisdom (Hikmat, Sophia).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01741

Among philosophers, Intelligence is generally associated with the Pen, while the Soul (Nafs) is associated with the Tablet. Here, by contrast, Intelligence is the Tablet, receiving within pure Luminosity the totality of the influences and outpourings of the divine Emanator (al-mofîd al-haqq). Pen, Inkwell, Ink, Tablet: these, then, are the symbolic names of the fourfold group of awwaliyât, the first realities. Together they constitute the Emanation through the act of bestowing existence (fayz ijâdî), while from Intelligence, the Tablet, proceeds the Emanation through the divine Command (fayz amrî).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01742

These stages in the unfolding of being directly govern the structure and methods of interpretation, or ta’wîl, whose organs and degrees, as we have seen, are the subtle centers of mystical anthropology. It is important to recognize that metaphysical imagination understands the coming of being and the world into existence as a form of writing. There is the Pen that writes, the Inkwell that is the Spirit, the Ink that is Light, and the Intelligence that receives and preserves the Writing. Cosmology thus lends itself to interpretation in the same way as a text.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01743

Consequently, the interpretation (ta’wîl) of the Quran corresponds to the structure of the world and to that of the human being as microcosm. Interpretation progresses through seven esoteric depths because, in each mystic (sâlik, wayfarer), those depths correspond to the subtle organs of the mystic's own being. The deepening understanding of the seven inner meanings depends on the development of these subtle organs, which in turn determines the growth of the imperishable spiritual body. The keys that unlock inward meaning work equally for the revealed Book, the Book of the world, and the Book of the human being, because every part corresponds precisely to its counterpart.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01744

This correspondence, as we have just seen, begins with the awwaliyât. Each first reality is the projection of an Attribute of Light, itself the projection of an Attribute of Life. Each is the projection, “shadow” (zill), or manifestation (mazhar) of the attribute from which it proceeds, just as one light emanates from another.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01745

From their fourfold grouping, in turn, emanate the four “proto-substances.” (1) The Pen is the manifestation (mazhar) of Knowledge, which is itself the manifestation of Life. (2) The Inkwell, or Spirit, manifests Will, which manifests Hearing. (3) The luminous Ink manifests Power, which manifests Vision. (4) The substance of Intelligence is the manifestation of Wisdom, which is itself the manifestation of the Word, or Logos (Kalâm). (See the summary diagram below.)
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01746

These first realities already provide some of the elements whose influences enter into the formation of the seven organs of subtle physiology. This is why Semnânî needed a metaphysics of being that reached further back than the philosophers' ontology, seeking what makes the first substance itself substantial.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01747

Here the Pen stands to Intelligence as the soul stands to the body. The Spirit-Inkwell and the Light-Ink stand to Intelligence as Form and Matter stand to the human being. The substance of Intelligence is at once the fourth member of the four first realities and the unity of them all; as such, its unity is distinct from that of any member taken separately. It is the first letter, alif, arising from the other three awwaliyât.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01748

Thus it is simultaneously the fourth of the awwaliyât and the first of the “proto-substances” (jawharîyât). The metaphysical Writer (al-Kâtib al-haqîqî), using the secret Pen (Qalam khafî) and the luminous Ink hidden in the Spirit-Inkwell, inscribes upon this Tablet—Intelligence, which receives its successive emanations of light—all that exists in the Writer's pre-eternal knowledge and that the divine Will projects into manifestation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01749
II. The Proto-Substances (jawharîyât, literally “substantialities”)
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01750

The term refers specifically to the four emanations that proceed in turn from Intelligence. Each corresponds to, and is the form of manifestation (mazâhir) of, one of the first realities (awwaliyât), just as the first realities manifest the Attributes of Light, which in turn manifest the Attributes of Life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01751

The proto-substances provide the essential link in the coming-to-be of beings and of the cosmos. They form the transition, or mediation, between the absolutely simple first realities and compound natures in the full sense. The composition of the latter is called tarkîb. The proto-substances, by contrast, are still “relatively simple”: they combine in a subtler way, called ta’lîf (or i’tilâf), “consociation”—a joining together rather than ordinary physical composition.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01752

Semnânî's derivation of the four proto-substances offers a striking example of the kind of reasoning found in Avicenna's cosmology of angels, which we have already discussed here, especially in connection with Suhrawardî's Vade-mecum. At the same time, Semnânî's account has distinctive features that clearly set it apart. For Semnânî, as for Avicenna, it is through its acts of contemplation that Intelligence brings forth the beings emanating from it.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01753

But in Avicenna the first Intelligence's three acts of contemplation give rise, respectively, to the second Intelligence, the Soul of the first heaven, and the subtle matter of that first heaven. In Semnânî the three acts of contemplation produce the proto-substances, whose names and places in the order of being do not coincide with Avicenna's account.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01754
1) In Semnânî, Intelligence, through a first act of understanding that marks the “highest dimension” of its being, contemplates the one who gives it existence, just as it does in Avicenna.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01755

But instead of this contemplation giving existence to a second Intelligence, as in Avicennism, it produces the substantial reality of the Soul of the universe (Nafs kollîya). Since Intelligence is contemplating its Principle, it emanates this Soul through the mediation of the Pen, which manifests the attribute of Knowledge. In the hierarchy of proto-substances, then, the Soul is the “shadow” (zill), the manifestation (mazhar), of the Pen; and the Quranic vocabulary calls this Soul the Throne (’Arsh). The Pen, in turn, manifests Knowledge, an Attribute of Light, just as Knowledge manifests the supreme Attribute of Life—Life itself.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01756

2) In a second act of understanding, marking the “middle dimension” of its being, Intelligence contemplates its own being, as it results from its connection to the Principle that grounds its existence and makes that existence necessary. It therefore understands itself as entrusted with a vicegerent function, as the deputy (khalîfa) of the Principle from which it emanates. It is the organ of divine Emanation, appointed by the existence-giving Command (îjâzat-e amrî) to send forth that Emanation and convey it to all that lies below it.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01757

In Avicennism, this corresponds to the act by which Intelligence recognizes that the necessity of its existence comes not from itself but from its Principle, and through which it brings forth the first Anima caelestis, the Soul of the first heaven, or Soul of the universe. Here the difference in ordering appears again: unlike Avicenna's system, Semnânî derives the Soul of the world from Intelligence's first act of contemplation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01758

Moreover, his second act produces not the Soul of the world but the substantial reality of Forma prima, First Form, which is paired with the substantial reality that Intelligence's third act will give to Materia prima, First Matter.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01759

“First Form,” also called latîfa fâ’ilîya (the active subtle principle), is, in Semnânî's hierarchy of proto-substances, the shadow or manifestation of the first reality called the Inkwell. The Inkwell symbolically designates the Glorified Spirit (Rûh Ahmadi, the Muhammadan Spirit), which itself manifests Will, an Attribute of Light, just as Will manifests Hearing, an Attribute of Life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01760

3) Intelligence's third act of understanding corresponds once again to Avicenna's angelology, but with another shift. Intelligence perceives its own insufficiency: it cannot sustain itself in being; it does not possess in itself what it needs in order to exist.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01761

Thus, if it imagines itself separated from the Principle to which it owes the necessity of its existence, its being amounts only to the possibility of being, forever exposed to the possibility of nonbeing. The contemplation of this possible nonbeing, even though it is purely hypothetical, marks Intelligence's “lowest dimension.” For Avicenna, this is the dimension through which Intelligence emanates the still wholly subtle matter of the first heaven—the Sphere of Spheres—moved by the Soul of the world. For Semnânî, this act of contemplation produces not yet the matter of the first heaven, but the substantial reality of Materia prima: universal matter, still entirely subtle.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01762

We can therefore see quite clearly how the idea of a Materia prima common to all beings, spiritual as well as material, becomes indispensable to Semnânî's understanding. The idea of such “metaphysical matter” in a subtle state is already present in the neo-Empedocles known to Islamic philosophers. It emerges in Avicenna and is fundamental to Ibn ’Arabî. It allows Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî to develop his account of the imaginal world and of the human being's existence after death.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01763

In short, it makes possible a realism of the “concretely spiritual,” which has its counterparts among the Cambridge Platonists (spissitudo spiritualis) and the successors of Jacob Boehme and Swedenborg (Oetinger's geistige Leibhaftigkeit, or spiritual embodiment). We have already encountered the idea and shall encounter it again; there is no need to dwell on it here. We should nevertheless emphasize that “matter” and “form,” the defining concepts of Aristotelian matter-and-form theory, operate here in quite a different way from their operation in Aristotle's philosophy.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01764

The same will be true in Shaykhî gnosis, in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, where these very symbols—the Pen, Inkwell, Ink, and so forth—bear fruit and where the theory of matter and form likewise undergoes a complete transformation. The idea of total tajarrod (khôrismos, immateriality) is finally excluded—along with the false dilemma between “materialism” and “spiritualism” that it sustains. It is precisely this “spiritual realism” that Semnânî's conception of the subtle body and the physiology of its centers or organs requires.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01765

Materia prima is also called latîfa qâbilîya, the receptive or passive subtle principle. Within the hierarchy of proto-substances, it is the shadow and manifestation of the luminous Ink (madâd nûrî), another name for the Muhammadan Light (Nûr Mohammadî). That Light manifests Power, an Attribute of Light, just as Power manifests Vision, an Attribute of Life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01766

4) Finally, just as Intelligence completes the three first realities—the Pen, Inkwell, and luminous Ink—to form a group of four, constituting a distinct unity that contains and sums up the three within its own being, so a consociation (ta’lîf, distinct from physical composition, tarkîb) now takes place between the subtle substance of Materia prima and that of Forma prima. From it comes the first body: the body of the first heaven, composed of incorruptible “ether-like” matter. Once again we see Semnânî's “first philosophy” trying to grasp things at a level prior to the one philosophers ordinarily consider.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01767

Just as the being of Intelligence is prepared by the Inkwell and luminous Ink, which stand to Intelligence as form and matter stand to the body, so, before we can speak of the first heaven proceeding from Intelligence's third act of understanding, our account must already possess a Materia prima and a Forma prima. Their first consociation is precisely what produces that heaven. It is called the “Sphere of Spheres” (falak al-aflâk) when considered as the source of the daily movement of the other heavens: the movement from east to west, opposite to each heaven's own movement from west to east.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01768

As we have already observed, the intellectual meaning of such representations—their Imago mundi, or image of the world—remains what it is, whatever the subsequent development of astronomy. This heaven is called the “Crystalline Sphere” (Falak Atlas) when considered in its purity, its “single-colored” character (sâdhîjîya), since it has no constellations. It is also called the Korsî (firmamentum, the Lesser Throne). Counting upward from Earth, it is the ninth heaven; in the order of emanation, it is the first.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01769

Among the four proto-substances, the first heaven corresponds to Intelligence among the four first realities. The first heaven completes the threefold grouping of Soul, Materia prima, and Forma prima, making a group of four.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01770

Thus the first, or ninth, heaven is the manifestation of Intelligence, just as Intelligence manifests Wisdom, an Attribute of Light, and Wisdom manifests the Word, or Logos (Kalâm), an Attribute of Life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01772

English key to the diagram. At its center are the Point of Essence — Being, the Point of Oneness — Life, and the Point of Unity — Light, associated with the first descent. The next band shows the Attributes of Life (immanent): Life, Hearing, Vision, and the Word (the second descent). The following band shows the Attributes of Light (transitive, or directed outward): Knowledge, Will, Power, and Wisdom (the third descent).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01773

The First Realities are, respectively, the Pen; the Inkwell, identified with the Muhammadan Holy Spirit (Rûh mohammadî); the luminous Ink, identified with the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî); and Intelligence, the Tablet (al-Lawh). The corresponding Proto-Substances are the Soul of the universe (’Arsh, the Throne); First Form; First Matter; and the Sphere of Spheres (Korsî, the firmament), the envelope of the cosmic egg. The diagram's four radial divisions show the correspondence Life → Knowledge → Pen → Soul; Hearing → Will → Inkwell/Spirit → First Form; Vision → Power → luminous Ink/Light → First Matter; and Word → Wisdom → Intelligence/Tablet → Sphere of Spheres.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01774

The Sphere of Spheres, or first heaven, is therefore the first body in the order of “descent,” and the ninth in the order of “ascent.” It forms the shell of the cosmic egg and corresponds to the human being's original earthly body (jism maj’ûl). The eight heavens enclosed within the cosmic egg are the shadows or manifestations of the four first realities (awwaliyât) and the four proto-substances. They are the “subtle organs” of the macrocosm, the upper world (’olwîyât); in the lower world (sofliyât), the four Elements and four elementary Qualities are their shadows.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01775

The three kingdoms of Nature (mawâlîd) arise from their mutual activity and reciprocal influence. Just as the human natural body encloses, like a membrane, the developing form of the spiritual body, which frees itself by breaking through that membrane, so beyond the ninth Sphere lies what the Quran calls al-Ofq al-mobîn, the supreme, translucent horizon (81:23, the horizon where the Prophet saw Gabriel, the angel of Revelation, appear). Situated between the proto-substances—Soul, Forma prima, and Materia prima—and the first body, or Sphere of Spheres, this horizon corresponds to the human subtle body. It is what elsewhere is called the “eighth clime,” the world of Hûrqalyâ.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01776

Indeed, several hadith identify this “translucent horizon” with Paradise, whose inhabitants possess spiritual bodies. It lies “below the Throne” (’Arsh, here the Soul of the universe); the “vault of Paradise is the Throne of the Merciful.” This points directly to the other hadith already cited as evidence for the subtle embodiment of the blessed: within the crop of the Green Bird, their “Throne-bodies” (jism ’arshî) are the lamps (qanâdil) suspended from that Throne (see § 5 above).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01777
We can now say that all the elements of the cosmology and anthropology are in place.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01778
III. Mystical Anthropology, or the Physiology of the Subtle Body
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01779

We shall retain from this cosmology only the broad outlines that lead us toward mystical anthropology. Semnânî's method of exposition is distinctive. He does not reason dialectically from genus to species, but examines concrete cases and their particular properties—for example, the motion proper to each heaven, a motion that is not a distinguishing characteristic separating one species from others within a genus. He begins by posing two alternatives, proceeds through hypothetical propositions examining each possibility, and moves from affirmation to negation, allowing the scheme to advance by elimination.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01780

The overall course of cosmology is organized into three groups: (a) essentially simple realities—the four “first realities” described above; (b) relatively simple realities—the four proto-substances, whose combinations, through successive divisions and eliminations, produce the entire structure of celestial physics and the physics of the Elements; and (c) compounds in the strict sense (tarkîbât).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01781

The last group comprises either compounds formed exclusively from subtle celestial substances—if invisible to bodily eyes, these are the Angels that move the heavens; if visible, they are the stars—or compounds made from the Elements. Such beings may be compounded of just one Element, for example Fire (as in the case of the Jinn), or of all four Elements; in the latter case, they are the earthly products of generation (mawâlîd).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01782

An animal either possesses a subtle organism or does not. If it does, we have entered the particular domain of subtle physiology. Every human being possesses this subtle organism; but it may be luminous by nature, or it may not. The distinction is fundamental. For the subtle organism, enclosed in the “original body” (jism maj’ûl) as in a membrane, may fail to grow beyond the “size” of its two nonluminous centers—the first two—and remain stunted. Such a person is the spiritual “failure,” the “stillborn soul in the world beyond” of whom we spoke earlier. Or the subtle organism may attain its full stature and complete the cycle of mystical anthropology through resurrection.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01783

Here again, the scheme develops by hypotheses and successive eliminations. A rhythm of advance and retreat governs the blending, the joining together, of influences from the upper world with those of the elemental world; this rhythm determines every degree of being. The process begins with the world of the Jinn, when influences from beyond the heavens—those of Intelligence and Soul—combine with the substance of Fire alone. Combination with the element Earth begins the kingdoms of nature.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01784

The mineral and vegetable kingdoms result from the influences of the Spheres and planets; the animal kingdom from those of the heaven of the Fixed Stars and the Sphere of Spheres. It is only in the human being's subtle organism that the first influence from a source beyond the heavens—that is, beyond the Sphere of Spheres—becomes apparent. As we ascend through the levels of subtle physiology, that source draws ever closer to the center of being.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01785

We must remember, however, that the combination always involves the element Earth. The physiology of the subtle body describes and explains how Earth, through purely spiritual means, enters into combination with influences coming from beyond the heavens—those of the “first realities” and the proto-substances.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01786

The result is an organism that naturally eludes all “laboratory testing.” It is no longer the animal body studied by biology and physics, the body belonging to our “carbon cycle.” It involves a sublimation of the element Earth that can be expressed only in the language of alchemy—though this is, as with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, an alchemy of resurrection. Here lies the entire mystery: the advance of this alchemy of resurrection from one subtle organ to the next; the growth of the subtle body from one depth of inward meaning to another, from prophet to prophet, each prophet representing a particular latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01787

Semnânî works out this idea beautifully in his commentary on the Quran (see § 2 above). And there is no other experiential means of verifying it than the one Semnânî, following Najm Kobrâ, watches so attentively: the vision of colored lights corresponding to the color of the veil or covering of each subtle organ. The color of this aura tells the mystic how far the subtle body has developed. Semnânî recorded many such extrasensory perceptions in scattered notes throughout his works, often dating them with all the care of a Diarium spirituale, a spiritual diary.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01788
Here, then, is a brief outline of the formation of each of the seven latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01789

1) The fundamental distinction, as we read a few lines ago, is this: A) either the subtle organ is luminous in itself (nûrânî), or B) it is not. If it is not, then (a) either the latîfa has a particular color, or (b) it has none. This last possibility divides into two further cases, each defined by the influence received from the upper world. Case (b) corresponds to the first two latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01790

Each subtle center, in fact, receives influences from several sources. The quality of the resulting being depends on the proportions in which these influences mingle. The first level is defined by the influences received by the first latîfa. It marks the beginning of the “acquired subtle body,” enclosed within the jism maj’ûl (see § 5 above)—the “microcosmic egg.” The first possibility is a combination in which the prevailing influence comes from the Sphere of Spheres (Korsî, the firmament), joined by a lesser or secondary influence received directly from the Throne (’Arsh), that is, the Soul of the world, without passing through the Sphere of Spheres.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01791

At this level, the most elementary degree of “spiritual embodiment” is formed. This is the latîfa qâlabîya, whose role is to act as a “mold” for the subtle body as a whole. It marks the transition from the physical organism to subtle embodiment. This is the Adam of your being. Its covering, or aura, is smoky gray, sometimes a deep black. The person belonging to this latîfa—the person who never progresses beyond this elementary degree of spiritual embodiment—is nevertheless distinct from an animal. For within the membrane of the perishable body (jism maj’ûl) lies the embryo of the “newly acquired body,” which survives the destruction of the earthly body.
